title: Kabuliwala
text:
Mini was five years old and could not stop talking. One day she called out to a tall Afghan fruit seller passing in the street, a man from Kabul with a bag of dried fruit on his back. Her father, a writer in Calcutta, was afraid she would be frightened of him. Instead, within days, the Kabuliwala, whose name was Rahamat, and the little girl were the best of friends, laughing at their private jokes. He came every day and brought her almonds and raisins.

One morning Rahamat was led away by the police, his clothes stained with blood. A man had owed him money and denied it, and in the quarrel Rahamat had stabbed him. He was sentenced to years in prison.

Mini grew up and forgot him. On the morning of her wedding, Rahamat appeared at the door, just released. He asked to see her. Her father, busy and uneasy, put him off. Rahamat turned to go, then offered a few raisins and almonds for Mini, and took out a crumpled piece of paper. On it was the smudged print of a small hand. He had a daughter of his own in Afghanistan, he explained, and he had carried this mark of her hand all those years.

The father's eyes filled. He called Mini in her bridal clothes. Rahamat saw that she was grown, and realized his own daughter must be too. The father gave him money from the wedding budget so he could go home to her, and cut back the wedding lights and band.
lesson: Parents everywhere share the same longing for their children. Seeing that in a stranger can turn suspicion into kindness.
people: Rahamat the Kabuliwala, Mini, her father
